cards.title: Polynomial-time recognition of abelian cores
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite algebra \(\mathbf A\) by full tables of its basic operations and promised that \(\mathbf A\) has an idempotent Taylor term, decides whether the core of \(\mathbf A\) is abelian? This selects the decision part of Theorem 3, whose quasipolynomial running time is the subject of the source’s open question.

source_formulation.text: We do not know whether the quasi-polynomial time algorithms in Theorem 3 can be improved to polynomial time.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 5

cards.why: Measures the cost of recognizing algebraic structure that can make entire families of equation systems tractable. The question asks whether a useful structural classification can be found with polynomial preprocessing, rather than only being available as a theorem about each fixed algebra.
cards.status_note: Read the complete original question, Theorems 1–3, core and Taylor definitions, the matrix definition of abelianness, and Section 5’s quasipolynomial bound. Read the June 2024 overview’s meta-problem discussion. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no polynomial-time improvement for the stated promise problem. The decision branch is explicitly selected; no equivalence with the additional constructive outputs or with unrestricted equation solving is assumed.

progress.text: Theorem 3 establishes quasipolynomial abelian-core recognition for finite algebras with a Taylor term, with additional construction guarantees on positive instances.
A subsequent overview restates the quasipolynomial classification algorithm in the congruence-modular setting.

sentences: The input is an entire finite algebra specified by tables of its basic operations.
It is promised to possess an idempotent Taylor term, although no witness is supplied.
The task is to decide whether its smallest endomorphic image is abelian in the universal-algebraic sense.
A quasipolynomial-time recognition algorithm is known.
This is a classification problem for algebras, distinct from solving a particular list of term equations.

cards.definitions:
A finite algebra \(\mathbf A=(A;f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})\) has a nonempty explicitly listed finite universe and a finite signature. Each basic operation \(f_{j}:A^{r_{j}}\to A\) is supplied by its complete table, with its arity. Nullary operations, when present, specify distinguished constants. The universe size, number of operations and arities may vary with the input. Let \(L\) be the total binary length of this description. A large-arity operation is not given by a succinct circuit or program.

A term is an expression made from variables and the given operation symbols; interpreting it on \(\mathbf A\) gives a term operation. Constants not in the given signature are not automatically available as term symbols.

The Taylor promise means that there are an arity \(r\geq2\) and a term operation \(t:A^{r}\to A\) such that \(t(a,\ldots,a)=a\) for every \(a\in A\), and for every coordinate \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there are two tuples \(\mathbf u_{i},\mathbf v_{i}\in\{x,y\}^{r}\) with \((\mathbf u_{i})_{i}=x\), \((\mathbf v_{i})_{i}=y\), satisfying
\[t(\mathbf u_{i}(a,b))=t(\mathbf v_{i}(a,b))\qquad\text{for every }a,b\in A.\]
The choices of \(r,t\) and identities may depend on the algebra. This is what the source means by membership in a Taylor variety. A witnessing term or operation table is not supplied, and recognizing whether the promise holds is not part of the task.

An endomorphism of \(\mathbf A\) is a map \(h:A\to A\) preserving every basic operation:
\[h(f_{j}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r_{j}}))=f_{j}(h(a_{1}),\ldots,h(a_{r_{j}})).\]
It must also fix the interpretation of every nullary symbol. Its image is a subalgebra. A core is an endomorphic image minimal under inclusion among such images, equipped with the restricted operations. For finite algebras these cores are unique up to isomorphism; equivalently, every endomorphism of the core is an automorphism.

Abelianness here is the universal-algebraic term-condition property. A concrete definition uses the algebra of \(2\times2\) matrices over a finite algebra \(\mathbf B\), with each basic operation applied entrywise. Let \(M_{\mathbf B}\) be the smallest subset of \(B^{2\times2}\) closed under these operations and containing all matrices
\[\begin{pmatrix}a&a\\ b&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}c&d\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\qquad(a,b,c,d\in B).\]
Then \(\mathbf B\) is abelian if every matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}x&y\\ z&w\end{pmatrix}\in M_{\mathbf B}\) satisfies \(x=y\Rightarrow z=w\). This is the source’s condition \([1_{\mathbf B},1_{\mathbf B}]=0_{\mathbf B}\). It is not a requirement that each basic operation be commutative.

One uniform deterministic algorithm must run in \(O(L^{k})\) bit operations for a fixed constant \(k\), with a fixed multiplicative constant, on all inputs. It must answer correctly for every well-formed algebra satisfying the Taylor promise. On other inputs the answer is unrestricted, but the polynomial time bound still applies. The requested output is only YES or NO; no particular representative of the core has to be chosen.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm with a uniform polynomial bound in the full table encoding length that recognizes abelian cores on every promised input, or prove that none exists. A conditional lower bound must identify its assumption. The source also asks for faster construction of the core and its Mal’cev operation in positive cases; those are additional output tasks and are not silently asserted equivalent to the selected decision question.

context_blocks.title: The source already gives a quasipolynomial algorithm
context_blocks.text: Theorem 3 decides abelianness of the core for every finite algebra in a Taylor variety. In positive cases it also computes the core and the table of its Mal’cev term operation. The open continuation asks whether the quasipolynomial algorithms can be made polynomial. The present card isolates recognition as one precise component.

context_blocks.title: Why the property matters for equation solving
context_blocks.text: Under the stronger congruence-modular assumption, Theorem 2 identifies abelian cores as the tractable side of the dichotomy for systems of term equations over a fixed algebra; the other side is NP-complete. This explains the recognition problem’s motivation. Theorem 3 itself has the broader Taylor promise, so that stronger assumption must not be substituted into its input specification.

context_blocks.title: Recognizing the promise is a separate problem
context_blocks.text: The source notes that testing for a Taylor term on an arbitrary finite operation-table algebra is EXPTIME-complete. Here its existence is promised. Conversely, the not-necessarily-idempotent Taylor polymorphism used elsewhere in the paper’s general CSP dichotomy is a different notion from the idempotent Taylor term in this promise.

context_blocks.title: The subsequent overview retains the quasipolynomial result
context_blocks.text: Aichinger’s June 2024 lecture on equations over finite algebras restates Mayr’s quasipolynomial recognition bound when discussing the congruence-modular case. It distinguishes the problem of classifying a supplied algebra from solving equations over a fixed one.

cards.context:
Theorem 3 decides abelianness of the core for every finite algebra in a Taylor variety. In positive cases it also computes the core and the table of its Mal’cev term operation. The open continuation asks whether the quasipolynomial algorithms can be made polynomial. The present card isolates recognition as one precise component.

Under the stronger congruence-modular assumption, Theorem 2 identifies abelian cores as the tractable side of the dichotomy for systems of term equations over a fixed algebra; the other side is NP-complete. This explains the recognition problem’s motivation. Theorem 3 itself has the broader Taylor promise, so that stronger assumption must not be substituted into its input specification.

The source notes that testing for a Taylor term on an arbitrary finite operation-table algebra is EXPTIME-complete. Here its existence is promised. Conversely, the not-necessarily-idempotent Taylor polymorphism used elsewhere in the paper’s general CSP dichotomy is a different notion from the idempotent Taylor term in this promise.

Aichinger’s June 2024 lecture on equations over finite algebras restates Mayr’s quasipolynomial recognition bound when discussing the congruence-modular case. It distinguishes the problem of classifying a supplied algebra from solving equations over a fixed one.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
